doc.title: Bernard Purdie interviewed by Monk Rowe, West Orange, New Jersey, July 30, 2003

title: Building rhythms around the singer; Aretha Franklin dates
summary: Without horns and strings present, Purdie built rhythms and counterrhythms around the singer's melody, citing Aretha Franklin hits.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

In those days when everybody was there on the session, did that include the singer?

Okay. So you really got to hear how what you were playing and what the rhythm section was playing was interacting with the whole thing. Now years later when all this is done in sections, is it different? Because you may not ever hear those horn parts and those string parts.

That’s right. So what I had to do was figure out what the arrangement was going to do. This is where my creativity came in. This is how I really became the star of all those recordings and things in the late sixties, seventies. Because I was creating part of the rhythms and the melody and the counterrhythms that was going to be set up for horns and strings and background singers.
Well how did you get to know where that was going to come in?

Because the singer would be there on the date. They would let them sing as we were running and rehearsing the song down. So I now got part of the melody. I got now the melody. Okay, I see where you want to go. And now it’s time for me to take the rhythm section and build the rhythm section around the melody and to become part of — for the singer to be center, and then build all these different kind of rhythms and counterrhythms around it. So yes, I became very intricate — a very intricate part of what the song would be. And the drums became very important. Bass became even more important. Guitars became even more. And of course the keyboard wasn’t just the piano anymore, they got some synthesizers and organs being put on. So yes, my influence was very, very heavy into what was going on. Because then I really learned how to put all this music together. Now I became an arranger, not only — I became a writer, arranger, producer. I really became all of those. But yet I wasn’t around when the horns were put on. I wasn’t around when the strings were put on. But what we had put down within the realm of the rhythm section laid the foundation for everybody else to sit on the throne with us. Because then I really was driving the vehicle.
That’s very interesting. So often times you might not hear the final product. You might be in your car driving along and the first time you hear that song that you played on might be on a car radio?

Yeah. And to give you a good example, one of the best examples in the world is Aretha Franklin. “Oh Me Oh My,” “Until You Come Back to Me,” I mean I can — “Rock Steady,” “Daydreaming,” “Think.” I mean all these things happened after the rhythm section was put down.
